Draw each continuous predictor as a straight line and as a spline

Source: R/splines.R
mm_splines.Rd

A diagnostic for the degrees of freedom a continuous predictor is given. Fitting one as a straight line is a modelling decision exactly as much as fitting it with a spline, and it is the decision this package makes by default and says nothing about: nonlinear is NULL unless an analyst names the predictor. This function makes both allocations visible and quantifies what choosing between them changes.

Usage

mm_splines(
  project,
  cohort,
  predictors = NULL,
  knots = 4L,
  at = NULL,
  n_points = 120L,
  plot = TRUE
)

Arguments

project

A mm_project().

cohort

The cohort. Development rows only, under the same eligibility rule mm_model() fits under.

predictors

Which continuous predictors to draw. Defaults to all of the project's that can carry a spline.

knots

Knots for the spline arm, as mm_model() takes them.

at

Reference profile, as a one-row data frame or a named list. The default holds continuous predictors at their median and categorical ones at their most common level, and the profile used is returned.

n_points

Points at which each curve is evaluated.

plot

Draw the panels. FALSE returns the curves and draws nothing.

Value

An object of class mm_splines: curves, one row per predictor and evaluation point with the risk each allocation implies; summary, one row per predictor with the degrees of freedom and the largest risk gap between the two; and the reference profile they were drawn at.

Details

It decides nothing. For each continuous predictor it fits the model twice, once with that predictor linear and once with it splined, everything else held as specified, and reports the predicted risk each implies across the predictor's observed range.

Why there is no test here, and no recommendation

Fitting a spline, reading the aggregate nonlinear term's p-value and dropping back to a straight line when it is not significant is a pretest estimator: the model's shape becomes a function of the outcome, and the optimism of that choice is corrected by nothing downstream. It is the same error as choosing interactions on the development data and then validating the chosen model as though it had been prespecified. rms::anova() prints the aggregate nonlinear row immediately beside the block test, so the temptation is one glance away.

The allocation belongs in the analysis plan, decided on what the predictor is rather than on what this cohort's outcome does. Harrell's advice is to spend the degrees of freedom by prespecification, more on predictors expected to matter, within the sample's budget. What this function supplies is the arithmetic for that conversation: the degrees of freedom each allocation costs and the largest risk difference between them.

What is plotted, and what is deliberately not

Both curves are adjusted: every other predictor is held at the reference profile, so the two curves differ only in how this predictor enters. A binned observed event rate is not drawn over them, however natural that looks, because a marginal event rate and an adjusted curve are different quantities and the eye would compare them anyway. A rug of the observed values is drawn instead, which is comparable: it shows where the data actually is, and therefore which parts of either curve rest on nothing.

Examples

cohort <- mm_synthetic_cohort(n = 600, prevalence = 0.15, seed = 1978)
project <- mm_project("uds", "event", c("age", "bmi", "sex"),
                      positive_class = 1, cohort = cohort)
shapes <- mm_splines(project, cohort, plot = FALSE)
shapes$summary
#>   predictor parameters_linear parameters_spline added_parameters
#> 1       age                 3                 5                2
#> 2       bmi                 3                 5                2
#>   largest_risk_gap at_value
#> 1       0.29929645     23.5
#> 2       0.09517398     48.6
#>                                                                                       note
#> 1 drawn over the observed range 23.5 to 95, every other predictor at the reference profile
#> 2 drawn over the observed range 15 to 48.6, every other predictor at the reference profile
